messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
Bram lets his pack slide off his shoulder onto the bench and props his shield against the wall within reach of his hand. He takes the chair with his back to the wall, where he can see the door and the stairs. Dust comes off his coat when he sits.

"Ale, whatever's drawn freshest," he tells the proprietor. "And something hot if your cook has it, I've eaten nothing since Nashkel but hardtack."

He sets a copper on the table, then looks at the two others in turn, not hurrying.

"Bram Halloway. I guard wagons, or I did until my last caravan paid me off yesterday. If you're waiting on someone, I'll not keep you company longer than the ale lasts." He tips his head toward the shutters. "The road from Nashkel was quiet this week. Quiet roads make me nervous, so I'm asking if anyone else here came in that way and saw anything worth remembering."

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa sets the Book of Shadows on the table beside her cup and lets her gaze move over the room, the proprietor, the two strangers, the door, without hurrying any of them.

"I'll take the seat by the shutters, if no one's bought it," she says to the room, and sits without waiting for an answer. Her fingers stay loose on the book's worn cover. "A cup of small beer, and whatever bread you have that isn't yesterday's. My thanks."

She nods to the proprietor, then turns a friendly, tired smile on the two others. "I walked up from the Gate, and I've been looking forward to a table that doesn't move under me. You came from the road too, I'd guess. Nashkel, or somewhere west?" Her eyes rest for a moment on the mud-stained boots of the man across from her, then lift to his face. "I'm Sefa. I'd rather know who's sharing the bread than sit here pretending I don't wonder."

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text: Pell takes the stool with its back to the wall, where he can see the door and both shutters, and sets the satchel on his knee rather than under the table. He nods to the proprietor. "Ale, whatever's cheapest that won't kill me. And a bowl of whatever's in the pot." He turns a copper over on the table with one finger, then looks along the bench at the other two. "Pell. I came in by the High Hedge, if anyone's wondering. Nobody's said a word yet, so I'll assume you're all as tired of the road as I am. Who's waiting on whom?"

scenes.narration:
Doran Quill takes Bram's copper without looking at it, drops it into his apron, and goes through to the back. He returns with a jug, a cup, and a bowl of barley stew that smells of onion and smoke, and sets them where they belong without a word wasted.

"Ale's from this morning's barrel. The stew's mutton, what's left of it. Hot enough." He sets the small beer and a heel of brown bread in front of Sefa. "Bread's today's. Only the crust is yesterday's, and you'll know which bit that is."

Bram's question gets the longest answer. Doran wipes his hands on the cloth over his shoulder and considers the shutters before he speaks. "Quiet, you say. Quiet's the word for it. A carter came in last night from the south, sat where you're sitting, and wouldn't say what road he'd come by. Drank half his ale, then went out to his cart and didn't come back for his change. I didn't ask. Nobody asks on this road any more." He glances at the door, then back. "Nashkel, you said? Then you'll know more about it than I do."

To Pell he gives a short shrug. "Nobody's waiting on anybody, as far as I can see. You three came in within the same quarter hour and haven't bought each other a drink, so I'd call you strangers. That's fine. Strangers pay the same as anyone." He turns back toward the bar, then stops and adds, not turning round, "Shout if the stew's bad. I'd rather hear it from you than from the street."

The lamps are not yet lit. The forge smoke thins over the rooftops, and the room settles into the low talk of people who have nothing to do but eat.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa tears the crust from the bread and sets it aside, as Doran asked, then lifts her cup to the room before drinking.

"Not Nashkel, I'm afraid. I came up from the Gate by the Trade Way, through the Friendly Arm and on to here," she says to Bram. "The road was quiet enough. A Flaming Fist patrol was loitering outside the Arm, six or seven of them, bored and sunburnt, and they looked me over the way Fist men look at anyone without a sword. Nothing else worth remembering, unless you count the Arm's ale, which I'd not count at all." Her mouth tilts. "If the roads are quiet, it's perhaps because the people who'd make them loud are waiting for something."

She turns her head toward Pell and lets her gaze rest on the satchel across his knee. She doesn't look at it long.

"The High Hedge, you said. I've never come that way, and I've heard it's all brambles and bad temper. Did it hold up?" Her voice stays easy and warm. "And you, Pell, have you been waiting on the company of strangers, or only on the stew?"

She sets her cup down and lays one hand flat on the Book of Shadows, not hiding it, simply resting it there.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell lets the first mouthful of stew go down before he answers. It's hot and tastes of onion, and he decides it will do.

"Nobody saw anything on the High Hedge worth the name," he says to Bram. "Sheep. A ferryman who wanted two coppers to take a dry cart across a dry ditch. But I came over the top of the Hedge at dawn, so I was above the road for most of it." He tips his head toward the shutters. "Two wagons a long way off, going south on the Trade Way, nowhere near a village. Didn't look like they were in a hurry, and didn't look like they'd stopped for anybody either."

He looks at Bram's coat, then at the dust on it, and his eyes don't stay long.

"You said your last caravan paid you off yesterday. Paid you in full, or did they pay you the way the carter paid Doran?" He nods at the seat by Sefa, where the drink was left half-finished. "Man who won't stay for his change is either honest about being in a hurry or about being somewhere he shouldn't be. I've never found much difference."

He turns to Sefa then, and his voice is no warmer, but it is more direct. "And you walked up from the Gate. Did you come through the Friendly Arm, or did you go round it?" He lifts his cup and drinks, watching her over the rim. "You're carrying a book you don't read in front of people. I'd like to know what's in it before I decide whether you're worth sitting next to."

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
Bram takes the stew and eats a spoonful before he answers Doran. "It's good. Better than the Friendly Arm's, and I've had their mutton."

He sets the spoon down and turns his cup slowly on the table. "A carter who won't say which road he came by, and leaves his change. I've seen that before, mostly on the Way the week before a wagon goes missing." He looks at Doran. "Did his cart have a canvas over it? Mud on the wheels, or dust? And was he alone?"

Then he glances at the other two, not hiding that he is watching them. "Sefa, you came down from the Gate. Pell, you came in by the High Hedge. Neither of you has said you saw anything on the road. I'm not asking for your business. I'm asking whether you passed any wagons, or any men standing about where they had no reason to be, between here and wherever you started."

He doesn't reach for the satchel on Pell's knee, but his eyes rest on it a moment before they move on.

"I'll tell you what I know, so nobody thinks I'm fishing for nothing. The caravan I came up with last came through the Beregost stretch on Tenday and camped where the old well is. There were two wagons out of Beregost that had been meant to meet us at Nashkel and never came. Nobody in Nashkel had heard of them. The mine foreman said the Fist would look into it when the Fist had men to spare, which means never."

He picks up the bread, tears a piece, and waits.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell watches the sergeant's back all the way to the door, and only when it's gone does he pick up his spoon again.

"Waiting on the stew," he tells Sefa. "The Hedge was sheep and bad ditches, like I said." He tips his head at the satchel on his knee. "Healing. Three potions. I get paid to be the one who reaches people fast, and that means I carry what they might need before they know they need it. Doesn't make it a secret, just a job."

He gives her a level look, the sort that gets weighed rather than trusted. "Your book stays shut, you keep your hand on it, and I'll keep my satchel where it is. Fair enough for a shared table."

Then he turns to Bram. "Two wagons, a day or more overdue, and a mine foreman who won't send men after them." He sets down the spoon. "A sergeant who hears 'wagons' and drops his drink is either a man who knows something about them or a man who doesn't want to be asked. Nobody's asked him yet. Did you see which way he went out?"

He doesn't wait for the answer. Under the table, his fingers are already turning the copper over, and his eyes are on the door.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
Bram watches the sergeant's back until the door swings shut behind him. Then he finishes the spoonful of stew in his hand before he speaks.

"In full," he tells Pell. "Silver, counted on the foreman's table with me watching. Nobody in Nashkel pays a guard late, because they know the guards talk." He sets the spoon down. "I'd rather not be the man who tells a story to a Fist sergeant over his supper, but I suppose I've done it now."

He turns to Pell. "Those two wagons you saw. Which way were they facing? North toward the Gate, or south toward Nashkel? And how far off the road?"

To Sefa he says, more quietly, "The Arm's patrol. Did they stop you, or only look? If the Fist are sitting on the Arm and not out on the road, somebody has told them to watch the inn and not the wagons, and I'd like to know who."

He pushes the bread across the table toward her, since her crust was the only thing on the plate that was not stale, then leans back in his chair with his eyes on the door the sergeant left by.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa lifts her eyes from the book to the bar and watches the sergeant's back as he goes out. Then she turns back to the table and smiles at Pell, the smile of someone who has been asked a fair question and means to answer it fairly, if not fully.

"Ah, the book. It's my pact, and I don't read it aloud in taverns, the same way I wouldn't sing in a sickroom." Her fingers stay flat on the cover. "It holds the words I need when I need them, and a few I'd rather not explain over mutton. You may judge me by the bread I share. I've not come to cheat anyone at this table."

She tips her head toward the door where the sergeant vanished. "I didn't come through the Friendly Arm by choice, so I'll say that much. I went through it, drank their poor ale, and kept walking. And I'd sooner not sit beside a man who has a sergeant's leather at the bar and then leaves when a stranger says the word *wagons*. Bram, that was you, I think. Who is that man, do you know?"

She lowers her voice a little, though not much.

"Two wagons that never reached Nashkel. Did their drivers have families in Beregost, or only debts? Because if that sergeant was counting coppers at the wrong table just now, I'd like to know whose debts they were."

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
Bram turns his head toward the shutters and watches the empty step for a moment before he answers Pell.

"He looked south first. Down toward the ford, where the Nashkel road leaves the town. He stood there longer than a man does when he's only deciding where to get his supper. Then he went north up the forge street." He turns the cup a quarter turn on the table. "So he's either watching the road south or he's been told to. Either way, I wouldn't go looking for him at the Fist's lodging tonight."

To Sefa, more quietly: "I didn't know the drivers. I knew the caravan master who hired them, a man called Orrin Vale, and I'd trust him with my purse but not with my wife. I can't tell you whose debts they were. But two men who were meant to meet us at Nashkel and never came are either dead in a ditch or owing someone a great deal. Either way, somebody in this town will want to know where they went, and I'd rather it was us asking than someone else."

He looks back at Pell, and his voice stays level. "Which way were those wagons facing, Pell? And how far off the road? You didn't answer me, and I'd like to know before I decide whether you're a man who saw something or a man who only wants to sell me a tale."

He drinks the last of his ale, sets the cup down, and rests one hand flat on the table near his shield.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa breaks the heel of bread that Bram slid toward her and eats a small piece before she speaks. She keeps her voice low, pitched for the three of them.

"Three potions, and a paid runner who means no secret by it. Thank you, Pell. I'll keep my book shut." She taps the cover once. "Bram, the Fist didn't stop me at the Arm, they only looked, the way a dog looks at a bone it's not allowed. Someone had told them to watch the inn, and that means someone knew which road people were likely to take."

She glances at the smith's apprentice at the next table, who has gone back to his stew but keeps his eyes on the door.

"I don't know the forge men, but I know how to ask a frightened boy a question without frightening him further. Pell, Bram, if either of you wants the wagons' names and the names of whoever paid for them, I'll sit with that lad and buy him a second cup. I'll ask him where the drivers drank and whether anyone has come asking after them since. And I'll ask Doran who the sergeant drinks with, though I expect he won't say."

She sets the bread down and looks at Bram across the table.

"Does the company want that, or would you rather we each go our own way and meet again when we have something to trade?"

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell lets the sergeant's empty stool sit for a moment before he answers Bram.

"Trade Way, both wagons, heading south, and I mean heading south, not wandering," he says. "They were a long way off, maybe two miles past the last farm on the Hedge, and I was above them on the ridge with the sun behind me. I couldn't tell you how far off the road they were. Nearer the road than a wagon would sit if it had broken down." He turns his cup slowly on the table. "I didn't see drivers, or horses unhitched, or anyone waving. They weren't in trouble that I could see. That's the part I don't like."

He glances at the shutters, where the sergeant stood. "He looked south, toward the ford. Not at the road in front of him. Past it."

To Sefa, he shakes his head. "I don't know who they had at home, or whether they had any. But a driver with a family in Beregost goes to his wife's table when he's paid off, and a driver with debts goes wherever the debts tell him to. Your question's a good one. Doran's right about the forge, though. Ask there, and ask it quietly."

He finishes the stew, cold as it is now, and pushes the bowl aside. Then he reaches for the satchel on his knee and sets it on the bench beside him, where his hand can still find it without looking.

"Here's my offer, Bram. I'm not on anyone's road tomorrow and I've got nothing but a potion and a lantern to lose. If those wagons are still sitting out past the ford, I'd like to be the one who goes and looks before a Fist patrol does. I'll want a second pair of eyes, and I'll want to know what the foreman at Nashkel is paying, if anything. If you're not interested, say so and I'll finish my ale."

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa waits a moment for Bram, long enough to show him she isn't in a hurry to be answered. Then she picks up her cup and rises from the bench.

"Then I'll take that as yes, and as a fair trade of silences," she says quietly. "Pell, keep your satchel where it is. Bram, if you hear the name of the man who hired those drivers, or the house that's holding their debts, I'd like to know it before I'm asked about it by someone with less patience than you."

She crosses to the next table with the easy step of a woman who has spent years on wards and doorways, and sets her cup down near the apprentice's elbow without spilling a drop. She doesn't sit. She simply leans on the back of the bench across from him, as if she belonged there.

"That stew's gone cold on you, and your friend's right to kick you. Eat it, and I'll buy you the second cup, and you'll tell me nothing you don't want to." She smiles, and keeps her hands where he can see them, resting on the Book of Shadows. "I'm not from the Fist, and I'm not from the Guild. I've only come up the road to find out who's been paying men to make wagons disappear. Where did the drivers drink, the two from Beregost? And has anyone come asking after them since?"

messages.text:

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
Bram looks at Pell for a long moment, then at the copper under the cup, and his hand stays flat on the table.

"Two miles past the last farm, moving south in earnest, and not in trouble. That's what you've been trying to tell me." He nods slowly. messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa nods slowly, as though the boy has told her the price of bread and no more. "Thank you, Hob. Your name stays in this room, and I'll not say where I heard it, not to Doran or the Fist or anyone in a good cloak." She tucks the copper's worth of thanks into a smile and sets the cup near his bowl. "The man who came to the forge. Did he have a scar, or a ring, or a way of speaking? Any small thing you noticed and didn't think worth mentioning?"

She straightens and turns her head toward Bram without raising her voice. "Tamsin's, behind the forge row, with the carters in the back room. And Hallam's boy at the east yard, for the book that costs money to read. Which do you want first, Bram? I'd sooner go to the brew-house with someone who's been in a fight this week than alone, and I've never once been to a brew-house without wanting to leave by the back door."

Her hand rests on the Book of Shadows, and she waits, cup in her other hand, for Bram's answer.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
Bram shoulders the shield and lets his eyes go once around the room: the apprentice, the bar, the door Pell went out by. He does not follow Pell. A man who walks out into dusk without his change has his own reasons, and Bram has no quarrel with him yet.

He sets a copper beside Doran's cup. "For the stew, and for the yard. You didn't say his name, and I won't either."

Then he crosses to the next table, not hurrying, and stops a little way from Sefa so the apprentice can see him without feeling watched. He keeps his voice low and easy.

"Son, I'm not the Fist, and I'm not Hallam. I'm a man who drove a wagon up that road for ten years. If your father or your uncle drives the south road, tell him a guard named Bram would like a word in the yard at Hallam's, before the lamps are out. He can say no. I'll still pay for the water either way."

He looks at Sefa, then toward the door Pell used. "Sefa, will you come east with me to the yard? Or do you want to keep your bread here where the stew's hot?"

scenes.narration:
Hob's spoon stops halfway to his mouth. He hears the name Sefa has used for him and goes very still, and he does not say whether it is his. His eyes go to the door first, then to the bar, where Doran is pouring, and his ears colour again.

"Dark blue coat," he says, pitched to his bowl. "Good wool. Not Beregost cut, the collar turned up. He had a silver ring on the right hand, and he kept turning it with his thumb while Corran talked." He swallows. "Talked like he was from Amn, or wanted you to think so. I didn't look at his face. Corran did. Corran don't say what he saw."

He hasn't finished, and he knows it. He breaks off and looks at the shutters, then pushes the cup back a finger's width towards Sefa, as if he has not decided whether to keep it.

Bram comes across the room and stops at a little distance, and the boy looks up at him properly for the first time.

"I don't have a father on the south road," Hob says, quick and flat. "I'm at Corran's. Forge boy. That's all." His voice drops further. "If Corran hears a guard came asking for the carters' lot, he'll have my wages and I'll be out on the road. So don't say my name in the yard. Please, I mean it, just don't say it."

At the bar Doran takes Bram's copper from beside his cup without looking at it, and drops it into his apron with the others. He sets the jug down. "Yard's open till the lamps are lit in the street," he says to the room, and turns to the hearth.

The lamp over the bar burns steady. Outside, the street has gone from dusk to the blue of full evening, and somewhere across the square a dog has started barking at nothing.

Bram has asked his question and is waiting for the answer. It is Sefa's to give.

presses.text:
The cloaked man keeps to the forge row, and the dusk does most of the hiding for both of you. Pell stays close to the house walls, stopping when the man stops, moving when he moves.

Halfway along the row, a lantern hangs over a shuttered cooper's yard. In its light Pell sees the man meet someone coming the other way: a thin figure in a hooded tabard, the sort a drover wears to market. They don't shake hands. The hooded man says something short, and the cloaked man nods once, turns his ringed hand palm-down, and then looks back over his shoulder toward the square. Pell is already in the shadow of a water butt, and the glance passes over him.

The hooded man walks off north toward the Fist's lodging. The cloaked man goes on east, toward the forge row's end, where the road leaves the town for the south-east fields.

Pell's Perception has caught something else, too. Under the drover's tabard, the hooded man has a belt of tools, neatly kept, and the tabard's sleeve is stained at the wrist with something dark. It might be ink, or it might be blood a day old.
presses.reply:
The cloaked man's ring catches the lantern once more as he turns away from the cooper's yard, and then the dusk takes the light and both men with it. Pell has seen what there was to see: the nod, the hand turned palm-down, the glance back toward the square that passed over the water butt without stopping.

The hooded man in the drover's tabard does not look back at all. He goes north up the forge row toward the Fist's lodging, his stride even and unhurried. Where the sleeve has fallen back at the wrist, the cloth is dark. Ink, perhaps, if he keeps tallies for a carter. Or something a day old that has not yet washed out. The belt of tools at his hip is kept too neatly for a drover: every loop full, every buckle polished.

The cloaked man goes on east, past the cooper's, toward the end of the row where the lanes thin into fields and the road for the south-east fields leaves the town. He does not hurry. Twice he stops where a shuttered window throws a line of light across the cobbles, and each time he waits, as if for someone who has not yet come.

Pell is still at the water butt, the cold of the stone coming through his coat. Two ways open from here. The cloaked man is heading out past the last houses, where a man can be gone in a minute. The hooded man is walking toward the Fist, where a tradesman with neat tools and a stained cuff would be asked a great many questions if anyone stopped him.

Which of them does Pell follow?

Where you are: at the table in the common room of the Burning Wizard · Time: Day 1 · afternoon

Sefa has taken the seat by the shutters, setting a worn book beside her cup and letting her eyes travel over the room, the proprietor, the two of you and the door before she settles. She asks for small beer and some bread that isn't stale, then smiles at you both as though she's glad of a table that stays still. She guesses you came up the road from Nashkel or somewhere west, and gives her name as Sefa.

Pell has taken the stool against the wall, where he can watch the door and both shutters, with his satchel on his knee instead of under the table. He orders the cheapest ale and a bowl of whatever's in the pot, sets a copper down, and gives his name as Pell. He came in by the High Hedge, he says, and he wants to know who is waiting on whom.

Doran Quill takes your copper without looking at it, drops it into his apron, and goes through to the back. He returns with a jug, a cup and a bowl of barley stew that smells of onion and smoke, and sets them down without a word wasted.

"Ale's from this morning's barrel. The stew's mutton, what's left of it. Hot enough." He sets small beer and a heel of brown bread in front of Sefa and tells her only the crust is yesterday's. Then he wipes his hands, looks at the shutters before he answers you, and says a carter came in last night from the south, sat where you're sitting, wouldn't say which road he'd used, drank half his ale and went out to his cart without collecting his change. Doran didn't ask him anything, and nobody asks on this road any more. He glances at the door. "Nashkel, you said? Then you'll know more about it than I do."

To Pell he gives a short shrug and says nobody seems to be waiting on anybody. The three of you came in within the same quarter hour and haven't bought each other a drink, so he counts you as strangers, and strangers pay the same as anyone. He turns back toward the bar, then adds over his shoulder that if the stew's bad you should tell him, since you'd rather hear it from inside than from the street.

The lamps are not yet lit. Forge smoke thins over the rooftops, and the room settles into the low talk of people who have nothing to do but eat.

Where you are: chair against the back wall, facing the door and stairs · Time: Day 1 · afternoon

Sefa says she came down from the Gate, through the Friendly Arm, and on to here. A Flaming Fist patrol of six or seven men was outside the Arm, and she thinks the roads are quiet because the people who would make them loud may be waiting for something. Her gaze rests on Pell's satchel, and she asks him whether the High Hedge held up and whether he has been waiting on company or only on the stew. She lays her hand flat on the Book of Shadows. Pell takes his first mouthful of stew before answering. He says the High Hedge had nothing worth remarking, only sheep and a ferryman demanding a fee to take a cart over a dry ditch. He came over the Hedge at dawn and saw two wagons far south on the Trade Way, going neither fast nor stopping. He looks at your coat and the dust on it, then asks whether your caravan paid you in full or the way the carter paid Doran. He glances at the seat by Sefa, where the drink was left unfinished, and says a man who won't wait for his change is either in a hurry or somewhere he shouldn't be. He asks Sefa whether she came through the Friendly Arm or around it, and tells her he would like to know what she carries before he decides whether she is worth sitting next to. Doran answers you: a grey canvas patched with sacking, a bay horse favouring its near fore, mud from wetter ground than the Way's dust, and the carter alone, with nobody at the door or the trough when he left. Doran says nothing more about the bread to anyone but Sefa. At the end of the bar a sergeant in leather hears you say wagons, looks at you for a long breath, then goes out into the dusk without finishing his drink. Doran lights the first lamp over the bar.

Your journal, new:
+ Thread: Two wagons that never reached Nashkel

Where you are: at the table, turning his cup · Time: Day 1 · afternoon

Pell has set down the spoon and asked whether you saw which way the sergeant went out. Pell says a sergeant who drops his drink at the word "wagons" either knows something about them or doesn't want to be asked, and that nobody has asked him yet. Pell has also said the Hedge was sheep and bad ditches, and that the satchel on Pell's knee holds three healing potions carried for people who might need them. Pell has warned Sefa to keep the book shut and a hand on it, and has promised to keep the satchel where it is. Pell's fingers are turning a copper under the table while Pell watches the door.

Sefa has said her book is a pact that holds the words she needs, and that she won't read it aloud in taverns. She has said she came through the Friendly Arm, drank their poor ale, and kept walking. She has asked who the man at the bar is, and she thinks you were the one who said the word. She has asked whether the drivers had families or debts, and says she would like to know whose debts they were if the sergeant was counting coppers at the wrong table.

Through the open shutters you watch the sergeant stop on the step and look south, toward the end of the Trade Way where the Nashkel road runs past the ford. He stands there a breath too long. Then he turns north up the forge street toward the Fist's lodging, and the dusk takes him.

Doran has been listening from the bar. He wipes his hands on the cloth over his shoulder. He doesn't know the sergeant's name. The man pays in full, drinks one cup, and comes in off watch to sit where he sat tonight. Doran doesn't know the drivers either; he says to ask at the forge or ask the Fist, not here. Then he goes back to the bread board and does not come near the table again.

Sefa's question stays unanswered. At the next table a smith's apprentice laughs, stops, and looks at the door. The lamp over the bar gutters and steadies. The stew has gone cold in two of the bowls. Outside, someone is shouting for a boy named Tam, and nobody at the table turns to see whether he comes. Pell's question to you is still open, and so is yours to Pell: which way the wagons were facing and how far off the road they sat.

Where you are: at the table in the Friendly Arm · Time: Day 1 · afternoon

Pell says he saw both wagons on the Trade Way, moving south in earnest, not drifting. From the high ridge, with the sun at his back, he judged them a long way out, maybe two miles beyond the last farm on the Hedge. He can't say how far from the road they sat, only that they were nearer it than a broken wagon would be. He saw no drivers, no unhitched horses, and no one waving for help. He says they didn't look like they were in trouble, and that is what troubles him.

Sefa has broken off a piece of bread and is listening. Quietly, you tell her you never knew the drivers, only the caravan master who hired them, a man named Orrin Vale. You'd trust him with your money but not with anything closer to home. You can't say whose debts the drivers carried. Two men who were due at Nashkel and never arrived are either dead in a ditch or owe someone a lot, and either way someone in Beregost will ask where they went. You'd rather it be you asking.

You look back at Pell and ask him again which way the wagons were facing and how far off the road they sat, since he hasn't answered. You want to know whether he saw something or only wants to sell you a tale. You drink the last of your ale, set the cup down, and rest one hand flat on the table near your shield.

Doran comes down the room with the jug before anyone calls for it and tops up your cup. He glances at the satchel on the bench beside Pell and says nothing about it. At the shutters the light has gone the colour of weak ale. "Mutton's finished," he tells the room. "Stew's what's left. Hot if you want it."

Sefa's question to the company hangs with the bread crust between you. The forge hammers have stopped for the day, and in the quiet the street sounds carry: a cart wheel, a woman calling a dog, a man laughing across the square.

Pell's offer lies on the table beside the satchel he has moved. He doesn't repeat it. His hand goes back to the copper under the edge of his cup, and it stays there. You haven't answered either of them yet. The lamp over the bar steadies, and the smith's apprentice has left his bowl half full.

Where you are: at the common-room table of the Beregost inn, by the shutters · Time: Day 1 · afternoon

Pell's copper has gone from under the cup, and Pell has stood up and left, the satchel still where his hand could reach it. Across the room Sefa has crossed to the next table and set her cup down near the apprentice's elbow, and she leans on the back of the bench across from him without sitting. The boy's hand comes out from under the table, and he speaks low to his bowl. You are too far off to catch more than a few words.

Pell stopped at the door, let the cold air into the room, and went out into the dusk. The shutters swung once and settled.

Sefa paid a copper for the boy's second cup, and he took it without looking at her.

You ask Doran your question as he passes with the pot. He stops, looks at the shutters, and answers without turning round. Hallam's yard, at the east end past the forge row, where the carters water their teams. You are to ask for his boy, not for Hallam, because Hallam keeps a book on everyone who comes up from the south and charges to read it. Doran asks you not to say his name inside. Then he goes on to the hearth.

The room has settled into its evening. The lamp over the bar burns steady, and the smith's apprentice eats his stew with his eyes on his bowl, his ear turned toward the table by the shutters.

Your journal, new:
+ Promise: Keep the apprentice's name out of it

Where you are: by the bench, shield on his arm · Time: Day 1 · afternoon

Hob's spoon stops halfway to his mouth, and the apprentice goes very still at the name Sefa has used. His eyes go to the door, then to the bar, then back to his bowl.

Sefa turns her head toward you without raising her voice. She names two places: Tamsin's, behind the forge row, where the carters drink in a back room, and Hallam's boy at the east yard, who has a book that costs money to read. She asks which you want first. She says she would rather go to the brew-house with someone who has been in a fight this week than go alone, and admits she has never once left a brew-house by the front door. Her hand rests on the Book of Shadows, and she waits, cup in her other hand, for your answer.

You cross to the next table and stop a little way from her, so the boy can see you without feeling watched. You speak low and easy. You say you are no Fist and no man of Hallam's, that you hauled freight up that road for ten years, and that if his father or uncle drives the south road, a guard named Bram would like a word in the yard at Hallam's before the lamps go out. The man can refuse, and you will pay for the water either way. You ask Sefa whether she will come east to the yard with you, or keep her bread here where the stew is hot.

"I don't have a father on the south road," Hob says, quick and flat. "I'm at Corran's. Forge boy. That's all." His voice drops. "If Corran hears a guard came asking for the carters' lot, I'm out on the road. So don't say my name in the yard. Please, just don't say it."

At the bar Doran takes the copper from beside his cup without looking at it and drops it into his apron. "Yard's open till the lamps are lit in the street," he says to the room, and turns to the hearth.

The lamp over the bar burns steady. Outside, the street has gone to the blue of full evening, and across the square a dog has started barking at nothing. Your question hangs in the air, and the answer is Sefa's to give.

messages.text:
Bram lets his pack slide off his shoulder onto the bench and props his shield against the wall within reach of his hand. He takes the chair with his back to the wall, where he can see the door and the stairs. Dust comes off his coat when he sits.

"Ale, whatever's drawn freshest," he tells the proprietor. "And something hot if your cook has it, I've eaten nothing since Nashkel but hardtack."

He sets a copper on the table, then looks at the two others in turn, not hurrying.

"Bram Halloway. I guard wagons, or I did until my last caravan paid me off yesterday. If you're waiting on someone, I'll not keep you company longer than the ale lasts." He tips his head toward the shutters. "The road from Nashkel was quiet this week. Quiet roads make me nervous, so I'm asking if anyone else here came in that way and saw anything worth remembering."

Bram takes the stew and eats a spoonful before he answers Doran. "It's good. Better than the Friendly Arm's, and I've had their mutton."

He sets the spoon down and turns his cup slowly on the table. "A carter who won't say which road he came by, and leaves his change. I've seen that before, mostly on the Way the week before a wagon goes missing." He looks at Doran. "Did his cart have a canvas over it? Mud on the wheels, or dust? And was he alone?"

Then he glances at the other two, not hiding that he is watching them. "Sefa, you came down from the Gate. Pell, you came in by the High Hedge. Neither of you has said you saw anything on the road. I'm not asking for your business. I'm asking whether you passed any wagons, or any men standing about where they had no reason to be, between here and wherever you started."

He doesn't reach for the satchel on Pell's knee, but his eyes rest on it a moment before they move on.

"I'll tell you what I know, so nobody thinks I'm fishing for nothing. The caravan I came up with last came through the Beregost stretch on Tenday and camped where the old well is. There were two wagons out of Beregost that had been meant to meet us at Nashkel and never came. Nobody in Nashkel had heard of them. The mine foreman said the Fist would look into it when the Fist had men to spare, which means never."

He picks up the bread, tears a piece, and waits.

Bram watches the sergeant's back until the door swings shut behind him. Then he finishes the spoonful of stew in his hand before he speaks.

"In full," he tells Pell. "Silver, counted on the foreman's table with me watching. Nobody in Nashkel pays a guard late, because they know the guards talk." He sets the spoon down. "I'd rather not be the man who tells a story to a Fist sergeant over his supper, but I suppose I've done it now."

He turns to Pell. "Those two wagons you saw. Which way were they facing? North toward the Gate, or south toward Nashkel? And how far off the road?"

To Sefa he says, more quietly, "The Arm's patrol. Did they stop you, or only look? If the Fist are sitting on the Arm and not out on the road, somebody has told them to watch the inn and not the wagons, and I'd like to know who."

He pushes the bread across the table toward her, since her crust was the only thing on the plate that was not stale, then leans back in his chair with his eyes on the door the sergeant left by.

Bram turns his head toward the shutters and watches the empty step for a moment before he answers Pell.

"He looked south first. Down toward the ford, where the Nashkel road leaves the town. He stood there longer than a man does when he's only deciding where to get his supper. Then he went north up the forge street." He turns the cup a quarter turn on the table. "So he's either watching the road south or he's been told to. Either way, I wouldn't go looking for him at the Fist's lodging tonight."

To Sefa, more quietly: "I didn't know the drivers. I knew the caravan master who hired them, a man called Orrin Vale, and I'd trust him with my purse but not with my wife. I can't tell you whose debts they were. But two men who were meant to meet us at Nashkel and never came are either dead in a ditch or owing someone a great deal. Either way, somebody in this town will want to know where they went, and I'd rather it was us asking than someone else."

He looks back at Pell, and his voice stays level. "Which way were those wagons facing, Pell? And how far off the road? You didn't answer me, and I'd like to know before I decide whether you're a man who saw something or a man who only wants to sell me a tale."

He drinks the last of his ale, sets the cup down, and rests one hand flat on the table near his shield.

Bram looks at Pell for a long moment, then at the copper under the cup, and his hand stays flat on the table.

"Two miles past the last farm, moving south in earnest, and not in trouble. That's what you've been trying to tell me." He nods slowly. "Wagons that are on schedule, on a road that's supposed to be empty, with nobody waving. I've seen that once before, and the men who were driving them were already dead."

He turns to Pell. "Your offer. Say it plainly. I'll hear it, but I'm not sitting down with a man who won't tell me what's in his satchel or what he wants for it."

To Sefa, quieter: "Orrin Vale keeps his books at the Nashkel yard, but he'll have a man in Beregost who knows his business. If the wagons were his, somebody in this town has had word of them. I'd like to find out who before the Fist decides it's nobody's problem."

He looks up at Doran as the man comes past with the stew. "Do you know a carter named Vale's man, or any teamster who runs the Nashkel road? A fellow who'd talk to a guard and not to the Fist?"

Then he finishes his ale and stands, shield in hand, and waits to see whether the others will come with him or stay to argue over the price of the stew.

Bram shoulders the shield and lets his eyes go once around the room: the apprentice, the bar, the door Pell went out by. He does not follow Pell. A man who walks out into dusk without his change has his own reasons, and Bram has no quarrel with him yet.

He sets a copper beside Doran's cup. "For the stew, and for the yard. You didn't say his name, and I won't either."

Then he crosses to the next table, not hurrying, and stops a little way from Sefa so the apprentice can see him without feeling watched. He keeps his voice low and easy.

"Son, I'm not the Fist, and I'm not Hallam. I'm a man who drove a wagon up that road for ten years. If your father or your uncle drives the south road, tell him a guard named Bram would like a word in the yard at Hallam's, before the lamps are out. He can say no. I'll still pay for the water either way."

He looks at Sefa, then toward the door Pell used. "Sefa, will you come east with me to the yard? Or do you want to keep your bread here where the stew's hot?"

The table was good. The Burning Wizard felt lived in, and Doran's economy of words made him easy to read. The two wagons are a hook I want to pull on, and the apprentice Hob gave us a real choice about whom to trust.

Two things I'd like handled differently next time. Some of the scene ran ahead of my actions: Pell left and Sefa crossed the room before I'd seen either happen, so I had to catch up on what had already changed. And I'd like to decide what Bram says and does myself, rather than have his words and his coin counted in the narration before I've spoken. Otherwise I enjoyed it, and I'm curious what Sefa answers about the yard and Hallam's book.

Yes, a few things. I wanted to press Pell about the satchel. He's carrying three healing potions and a good deal of nerve, and I never got a straight answer about where he'd been or why he was so keen to know what I carried. I also wanted to follow the sergeant. Bram would have gone out after him, or at least walked the forge street to see where he went, instead of letting him leave. Where you are: at the table in the common room of the Burning Wizard · Time: Day 1 · afternoon

Bram lets his pack slide off his shoulder onto the bench and leans his shield against the wall, close enough to his hand to grab. He settles into a chair against the wall, where he can see the door and the stairs, and dust shakes out of his coat as he sits. He asks for ale, whatever was drawn freshest, and something hot if the cook has it, since he has eaten nothing but hardtack since Nashkel. He sets a copper on the table and looks at each of you in turn, unhurried. He gives his name as Bram Halloway and says he guards wagons, or did until his last caravan paid him off yesterday. He says he won't keep you company longer than his ale lasts. The road from Nashkel was quiet this week, and quiet roads make him uneasy, so he asks whether anyone else came in that way and saw anything worth remembering.

Pell has taken the stool against the wall, where he can see the door and both shutters, and he has the satchel on his knee rather than under the table. He nods to the proprietor and orders the cheapest ale that won't poison him, along with a bowl of whatever's in the pot. He sets a copper on the table with one finger and looks along the bench at the two of you. He gives his name as Pell and says he came in by the High Hedge, in case anyone wonders. Nobody has spoken yet, he says, so he assumes you're all as weary of the road as he is, and he asks who is waiting on whom.

Doran Quill takes the copper without looking at it, drops it in his apron and goes through to the back. He comes out with a jug, a cup and a bowl of barley stew that smells of onion and smoke, and sets them down without a word. "Ale's from this morning's barrel. The stew's mutton, what's left of it. Hot enough." He sets a cup of small beer and a heel of brown bread in front of you, and says the bread is today's, only the crust is yesterday's, and you'll know which bit that is.

When Bram asks his question, Doran takes his time. He wipes his hands on the cloth over his shoulder and looks at the shutters before answering. A carter came in last night from the south and sat in the seat you have now. He wouldn't say which road he'd used, drank half his ale, went out to his cart and never came back for his change. Nobody asks questions on this road any more, Doran says. He glances at the door and then at Bram. "Nashkel, you said? Then you'll know more about it than I do."

To Pell he gives a short shrug. Nobody seems to be waiting on anybody. The three of you came in within the same quarter hour and haven't bought one another a drink, so he counts you as strangers, and strangers pay the same as anyone. He turns back toward the bar, then, without looking round, says he'd rather hear it from you if the stew is bad than from the street.

The lamps are not yet lit. Forge smoke thins over the rooftops, and the room settles into the low talk of people who have nothing to do but eat.

Where you are: seat by the shutters · Time: Day 1 · afternoon

Where you are: at the common-room table of the Beregost inn, by the shutters · Time: Day 1 · afternoon

Before you rose, Bram sat through your offer of silence and let it hang, then looked at Pell's copper under his cup and kept his hand flat on the table. He told Pell that the man was two miles past the last farm and moving south in earnest, not in trouble, and that wagons running to schedule on an empty road with no one waving were a sight he had seen once before, when the drivers were already dead. Lower, to you, Bram said the wagon owner, Vale, keeps his ledgers at the Nashkel yard but has a man in Beregost who handles his affairs, and that if these wagons were Vale's, someone in town must have heard of them. Then he turned his copper over in his palm, stood, left the satchel where his hand could reach it, and nodded to Doran. Sefa sets the Book of Shadows on the table beside her cup and lets her gaze move over the room, the proprietor, the two strangers, the door, without hurrying any of them.

"I'll take the seat by the shutters, if no one's bought it," she says to the room, and sits without waiting for an answer. Her fingers stay loose on the book's worn cover. "A cup of small beer, and whatever bread you have that isn't yesterday's. My thanks."

She nods to the proprietor, then turns a friendly, tired smile on the two others. "I walked up from the Gate, and I've been looking forward to a table that doesn't move under me. You came from the road too, I'd guess. Nashkel, or somewhere west?" Her eyes rest for a moment on the mud-stained boots of the man across from her, then lift to his face. "I'm Sefa. I'd rather know who's sharing the bread than sit here pretending I don't wonder."

Sefa tears the crust from the bread and sets it aside, as Doran asked, then lifts her cup to the room before drinking.

"Not Nashkel, I'm afraid. I came up from the Gate by the Trade Way, through the Friendly Arm and on to here," she says to Bram. "The road was quiet enough. A Flaming Fist patrol was loitering outside the Arm, six or seven of them, bored and sunburnt, and they looked me over the way Fist men look at anyone without a sword. Nothing else worth remembering, unless you count the Arm's ale, which I'd not count at all." Her mouth tilts. "If the roads are quiet, it's perhaps because the people who'd make them loud are waiting for something."

She turns her head toward Pell and lets her gaze rest on the satchel across his knee. She doesn't look at it long.

"The High Hedge, you said. I've never come that way, and I've heard it's all brambles and bad temper. Did it hold up?" Her voice stays easy and warm. "And you, Pell, have you been waiting on the company of strangers, or only on the stew?"

She sets her cup down and lays one hand flat on the Book of Shadows, not hiding it, simply resting it there.

Sefa lifts her eyes from the book to the bar and watches the sergeant's back as he goes out. Then she turns back to the table and smiles at Pell, the smile of someone who has been asked a fair question and means to answer it fairly, if not fully.

"Ah, the book. It's my pact, and I don't read it aloud in taverns, the same way I wouldn't sing in a sickroom." Her fingers stay flat on the cover. "It holds the words I need when I need them, and a few I'd rather not explain over mutton. You may judge me by the bread I share. I've not come to cheat anyone at this table."

She tips her head toward the door where the sergeant vanished. "I didn't come through the Friendly Arm by choice, so I'll say that much. I went through it, drank their poor ale, and kept walking. And I'd sooner not sit beside a man who has a sergeant's leather at the bar and then leaves when a stranger says the word *wagons*. Bram, that was you, I think. Who is that man, do you know?"

She lowers her voice a little, though not much.

"Two wagons that never reached Nashkel. Did their drivers have families in Beregost, or only debts? Because if that sergeant was counting coppers at the wrong table just now, I'd like to know whose debts they were."

Sefa breaks the heel of bread that Bram slid toward her and eats a small piece before she speaks. She keeps her voice low, pitched for the three of them.

"Three potions, and a paid runner who means no secret by it. Thank you, Pell. I'll keep my book shut." She taps the cover once. "Bram, the Fist didn't stop me at the Arm, they only looked, the way a dog looks at a bone it's not allowed. Someone had told them to watch the inn, and that means someone knew which road people were likely to take."

She glances at the smith's apprentice at the next table, who has gone back to his stew but keeps his eyes on the door.

"I don't know the forge men, but I know how to ask a frightened boy a question without frightening him further. Pell, Bram, if either of you wants the wagons' names and the names of whoever paid for them, I'll sit with that lad and buy him a second cup. I'll ask him where the drivers drank and whether anyone has come asking after them since. And I'll ask Doran who the sergeant drinks with, though I expect he won't say."

She sets the bread down and looks at Bram across the table.

"Does the company want that, or would you rather we each go our own way and meet again when we have something to trade?"

Sefa waits a moment for Bram, long enough to show him she isn't in a hurry to be answered. Then she picks up her cup and rises from the bench.

"Then I'll take that as yes, and as a fair trade of silences," she says quietly. "Pell, keep your satchel where it is. Bram, if you hear the name of the man who hired those drivers, or the house that's holding their debts, I'd like to know it before I'm asked about it by someone with less patience than you."

She crosses to the next table with the easy step of a woman who has spent years on wards and doorways, and sets her cup down near the apprentice's elbow without spilling a drop. She doesn't sit. She simply leans on the back of the bench across from him, as if she belonged there.

"That stew's gone cold on you, and your friend's right to kick you. Eat it, and I'll buy you the second cup, and you'll tell me nothing you don't want to." She smiles, and keeps her hands where he can see them, resting on the Book of Shadows. "I'm not from the Fist, and I'm not from the Guild. I've only come up the road to find out who's been paying men to make wagons disappear. Where did the drivers drink, the two from Beregost? And has anyone come asking after them since?"

Sefa lowers herself onto the bench beside the apprentice's friend, not across from the boy, and turns her cup slowly on the wood so he can see she's only holding it.

"Eat, lad. The stew won't argue with you." She waits until he picks up his spoon. "I'm buying the second cup whatever you say, so you needn't pay for the first with your tongue. I'm only asking where the Beregost drivers drank before they took the Nashkel road. The two from the wagons. Did they sit in a place like this one, or somewhere with a back door?"

Her voice stays soft and unhurried. "And has anyone come asking after them since? A man with money, or a man with a sword and no manners?"

The apprentice takes a spoonful of stew, chews it slowly, and looks at the cup in your hand rather than at you. Then he lowers his voice to nearly nothing.

"The Dripping Ewer, by the tanners' gate. Both of them, Tuesday night, they'd come in off the Nashkel road with their wagons in the yard." He glances at his friend, who has gone very still. "They drank at the back table, the one under the stair. They were laughing. One said he'd be rich by Nashkel and wouldn't have to look at a cart again." He swallows. "And yes. Before you rose, Bram sat through your offer of silence and let it hang, then looked at Pell's copper under his cup and kept his hand flat on the table. He told Pell that the man was two miles past the last farm and moving south in earnest, not in trouble, and that wagons running to schedule on an empty road with no one waving were a sight he had seen once before, when the drivers were already dead. Lower, to you, Bram said the wagon owner, Vale, keeps his ledgers at the Nashkel yard but has a man in Beregost who handles his affairs, and that if these wagons were Vale's, someone in town must have heard of them. Where you are: at the table in the common room of the Burning Wizard · Time: Day 1 · afternoon

Bram settles into a chair against the wall, where he can see the door and the stairs. Dust falls off his coat when he sits. He asks for ale and something hot, having eaten nothing since Nashkel but hardtack, and sets a copper on the table. He looks at each of you in turn, not hurrying. He gives his name as Bram Halloway and says he guards wagons, or did until his last caravan paid him off yesterday. He won't keep you company longer than his ale lasts. The road from Nashkel has been quiet, which makes him nervous, so he asks whether anyone else came in that way and saw anything worth remembering.

Sefa has taken the seat by the shutters. She sets a worn book beside her cup and lets her eyes move over the room, the proprietor, the two of you and the door without hurrying any of them. She asks for small beer and bread that isn't stale, and thanks the proprietor. Then she turns a tired, friendly smile on you both, says she walked up from the Gate and is glad of a table that doesn't move, and guesses you came from Nashkel or somewhere west. She looks down briefly at the mud on the boots of the man across from her, then up at his face. She gives her name as Sefa and says she'd rather know who is sharing the bread than sit there pretending she doesn't wonder.

Doran Quill takes the copper you set down without looking at it, drops it in his apron and goes through to the back. He returns with a jug, a cup and a bowl of barley stew that smells of onion and smoke, and sets them down without a word wasted. "Ale's from this morning's barrel. The stew's mutton, what's left of it. Hot enough." He sets small beer and a heel of brown bread in front of Sefa and says only the crust is yesterday's.

When Bram asks his question, Doran takes his time. He wipes his hands on the cloth over his shoulder and looks at the shutters before speaking. A carter came in last night from the south and sat in the seat Sefa has now, wouldn't say which road he'd taken, drank half his ale, went out to his cart and never came back for his change. Nobody asks questions on this road any more. He glances at the door and then at Bram. "Nashkel, you said? Then you'll know more about it than I do."

To you he gives a short shrug. Nobody seems to be waiting on anybody. The three of you came in within the same quarter hour and haven't bought one another a drink, so he counts you as strangers, and strangers pay the same as anyone. He turns back toward the bar, then, without looking round, says he'd rather hear it from inside if the stew is bad than from the street.

The lamps are not yet lit. Forge smoke thins over the rooftops, and the room settles into the low talk of people who have nothing to do but eat.

Doran answers Bram: a grey patched canvas, a bay horse favouring its near fore, mud from wetter ground than the Way, the carter alone. + Thread: Two wagons that never reached Nashkel

Where you are: at the table, satchel on his knee · Time: Day 1 · afternoon

Sefa has answered you with a wary look at the satchel on your knee; she says her book is her pact, that she doesn't read it aloud in taverns, and that she means no cheating at this table. Through the open shutters you see the sergeant stop on the step and look south, toward the end of the Trade Way where the Nashkel road runs out past the ford. He stands there a breath too long. Then he turns north up the forge street toward the Fist's lodging, and the dusk takes him.

Doran has been listening from the bar. He wipes his hands on the cloth over his shoulder. He doesn't know the sergeant's name and never asked. The man pays in full, drinks one cup, and comes in when he is off watch to sit where he sat tonight. Doran doesn't know the drivers. Sefa's question stays unanswered on the table. At the next table a smith's apprentice laughs at something his friend says, stops, and looks at the door. The lamp over the bar gutters and steadies. The stew has gone cold in two of the bowls. Outside, someone is shouting for a boy named Tam, and no one at the table turns to see whether he comes. Your question to Bram is still open, and so is his to you.

Where you are: at the table in the Friendly Arm · Time: Day 1 · afternoon

Bram has told the table that the sergeant looked south toward the ford first, stood there longer than a man deciding on supper, then went north up the forge street. He says the sergeant is either watching the south road or has been told to, and that you should not look for him at the Fist's lodging tonight. Bram also asked which way the wagons faced and how far off the road they were, and said he will decide whether you saw something or only want to sell him a tale. He drank his ale and set a hand near his shield.

Sefa has thanked you for the three potions and said she'll keep her book shut. She says the Fist didn't stop her at the Arm but only watched. Someone had set them to it, which means someone knew which road people would take. She glances at the smith's apprentice, who has gone back to his stew but keeps his eyes on the door. She offers to sit with the lad, buy him a second cup, and find out where the drivers drank and whether anyone has asked after them. She'll also ask Doran who the sergeant drinks with. Then she asks the table whether the company wants that, or whether they should each go their own way and meet again with something to trade.

Doran comes down the room with the jug before anyone calls for it. He tops up Bram's cup, glances once at the satchel on the bench beside you, and says nothing about it. At the shutters the light has gone the colour of weak ale. "Mutton's finished," he says to the room. "Stew's what's left. Hot if you want it."

The forge hammers have stopped, and the street sounds carry in: a cart wheel, a woman calling a dog, a man laughing across the square. The apprentice's friend kicks his boot under the bench, and the boy eats, slowly, with one ear on the table.

Your offer lies on the table beside the satchel you've moved to the bench. You don't repeat it. Your hand goes back to the copper under the edge of your cup, and it stays there. Bram hasn't answered yet. The lamp over the bar steadies.

messages.text: Pell takes the stool with its back to the wall, where he can see the door and both shutters, and sets the satchel on his knee rather than under the table. He nods to the proprietor. "Ale, whatever's cheapest that won't kill me. And a bowl of whatever's in the pot." He turns a copper over on the table with one finger, then looks along the bench at the other two. "Pell. I came in by the High Hedge, if anyone's wondering. Nobody's said a word yet, so I'll assume you're all as tired of the road as I am. Who's waiting on whom?"

Pell lets the first mouthful of stew go down before he answers. It's hot and tastes of onion, and he decides it will do.

"Nobody saw anything on the High Hedge worth the name," he says to Bram. "Sheep. A ferryman who wanted two coppers to take a dry cart across a dry ditch. But I came over the top of the Hedge at dawn, so I was above the road for most of it." He tips his head toward the shutters. "Two wagons a long way off, going south on the Trade Way, nowhere near a village. Didn't look like they were in a hurry, and didn't look like they'd stopped for anybody either."

He looks at Bram's coat, then at the dust on it, and his eyes don't stay long.

"You said your last caravan paid you off yesterday. Paid you in full, or did they pay you the way the carter paid Doran?" He nods at the seat by Sefa, where the drink was left half-finished. "Man who won't stay for his change is either honest about being in a hurry or about being somewhere he shouldn't be. I've never found much difference."

He turns to Sefa then, and his voice is no warmer, but it is more direct. "And you walked up from the Gate. Did you come through the Friendly Arm, or did you go round it?" He lifts his cup and drinks, watching her over the rim. "You're carrying a book you don't read in front of people. I'd like to know what's in it before I decide whether you're worth sitting next to."

Pell watches the sergeant's back all the way to the door, and only when it's gone does he pick up his spoon again.

"Waiting on the stew," he tells Sefa. "The Hedge was sheep and bad ditches, like I said." He tips his head at the satchel on his knee. "Healing. Three potions. I get paid to be the one who reaches people fast, and that means I carry what they might need before they know they need it. Doesn't make it a secret, just a job."

He gives her a level look, the sort that gets weighed rather than trusted. "Your book stays shut, you keep your hand on it, and I'll keep my satchel where it is. Fair enough for a shared table."

Then he turns to Bram. "Two wagons, a day or more overdue, and a mine foreman who won't send men after them." He sets down the spoon. "A sergeant who hears 'wagons' and drops his drink is either a man who knows something about them or a man who doesn't want to be asked. Nobody's asked him yet. Did you see which way he went out?"

He doesn't wait for the answer. Under the table, his fingers are already turning the copper over, and his eyes are on the door.

Pell lets the sergeant's empty stool sit for a moment before he answers Bram.

"Trade Way, both wagons, heading south, and I mean heading south, not wandering," he says. "They were a long way off, maybe two miles past the last farm on the Hedge, and I was above them on the ridge with the sun behind me. I couldn't tell you how far off the road they were. Nearer the road than a wagon would sit if it had broken down." He turns his cup slowly on the table. "I didn't see drivers, or horses unhitched, or anyone waving. They weren't in trouble that I could see. That's the part I don't like."

He glances at the shutters, where the sergeant stood. "He looked south, toward the ford. Not at the road in front of him. Past it."

To Sefa, he shakes his head. "I don't know who they had at home, or whether they had any. But a driver with a family in Beregost goes to his wife's table when he's paid off, and a driver with debts goes wherever the debts tell him to. Your question's a good one. Doran's right about the forge, though. Ask there, and ask it quietly."

He finishes the stew, cold as it is now, and pushes the bowl aside. Then he reaches for the satchel on his knee and sets it on the bench beside him, where his hand can still find it without looking.

"Here's my offer, Bram. I'm not on anyone's road tomorrow and I've got nothing but a potion and a lantern to lose. If those wagons are still sitting out past the ford, I'd like to be the one who goes and looks before a Fist patrol does. I'll want a second pair of eyes, and I'll want to know what the foreman at Nashkel is paying, if anything. If you're not interested, say so and I'll finish my ale."

Pell lets the question of the satchel go unremarked and watches Bram's hand near his shield. He doesn't reach for his own weapons.

"Fair enough, Bram," he says. "Don't take my word for the wagons. Go look yourself if you want to be sure, or sit here and let the Fist tell you what they found. I'll be going out past the ford at first light either way, with or without company."

He turns to Sefa. "Yes, get your lad his second cup and ask about the drivers. Ask about the sergeant too, quietly, and don't say you were asking for me. I'll take the Hedge road out at dawn and come back by the ford if I can. We meet here again tomorrow evening, and whoever has something to trade brings it to the table."

He picks up the copper from under his cup, turns it once, and drops it into his palm. Then he stands, leaves the satchel where his hand can reach it, and gives Doran a nod.

"Tell the cook the stew was good. It was better than it smelled."

He walks out past the shutters and into the dusk, keeping to the side of the street where the lamps are not yet lit.

Pell keeps to the wall until the shutters are behind him and the corner is between him and the inn door. Then he stops in the mouth of a narrow lane, where a stack of empty barrels makes a dark place to stand, and waits. He doesn't go far.

If anyone comes out after him, he wants to see who, and which way they turn.

He keeps his hand on the satchel strap and listens for boots on the cobbles, a door, a voice saying a name. He notes which of the Fist's men are on the street and which way they're walking, and he thinks about the Hedge road at first light, the ford, and whatever a Fist patrol might be waiting for out past it. He'll buy a fresh flask of oil at the smith's stall before the market shuts, if he can find one still open.

"Let them come to me," he mutters to himself, and then he crouches to look under the barrels.

Pell stays crouched behind the barrels and makes himself small. The square is going blue, and he can't yet tell a loiterer from a man waiting for his supper. He needs a better look before the lamps are all lit.

[Request an allowed reroll — Perception: reading the square from the barrels, who is watching the Burning Wizard's door]
[Roll the die]

The square comes apart into people as your eyes adjust. Two Flaming Fist men in leather walk the forge row together, turn at the corner, and walk it back again, never once stopping. Their pace is set by someone else.

By the dry well, a man sits on the low wall with a pipe he isn't lighting. He wears a drover's coat, too warm for the evening, and he has a good view of the Burning Wizard's door and the shutters. Twice he looks at the lamp over the bar. Once he looks at the lane where you are, and his gaze passes over your barrels without stopping.

Across the square, a boy with a basket is selling the last of the bread to the smiths' wives. He is watching the same door as the man at the well, and then he isn't, because a woman in a grey shawl has taken his attention. Nobody else in the square is doing anything they need to do.

You can't see the lane's far end from here, or the ford road. But you know now that the Burning Wizard has been watched since before you walked in, and that whoever watches it had no interest in the stew.

[Onward]

Pell pockets the flask of oil and keeps the cloak in view. "Good leather, and a ring he keeps touching," he murmurs. "Not a Fist man, not a drover. Somebody paid him to sit where he can see the door."

He lets the man get a good way ahead toward the forge row, then steps out of the barrels and follows at a distance, close to the house walls, where the dusk is thickest.

[Roll the die]

The cloaked man keeps to the forge row, and the dusk does most of the hiding for both of you. Pell stays close to the house walls, stopping when the man stops, moving when he moves.

Halfway along the row, a lantern hangs over a shuttered cooper's yard. In its light Pell sees the man meet someone coming the other way: a thin figure in a hooded tabard, the sort a drover wears to market. They don't shake hands. The hooded man says something short, and the cloaked man nods once, turns his ringed hand palm-down, and then looks back over his shoulder toward the square. Pell is already in the shadow of a water butt, and the glance passes over him.

The hooded man walks off north toward the Fist's lodging. The cloaked man goes on east, toward the forge row's end, where the road leaves the town for the south-east fields.

Pell's Perception has caught something else, too. Under the drover's tabard, the hooded man has a belt of tools, neatly kept, and the tabard's sleeve is stained at the wrist with something dark. It might be ink, or it might be blood a day old.

[Onward]

From my side it was a good first session. The three travellers each have a clear hook, Bram's wagons and Sefa's book give the table something to pull on, and the Burning Wizard felt like a real place with people who had their own business. The watchers in the square, the cloaked man and the hooded man with the ink-or-blood sleeve, were the kind of thing Pell is good at noticing, and I liked that the game let him find them without handing him the answer.

A few things I'd note for next time:

- The location kept shifting between the Burning Wizard, "the Friendly Arm" and "the Beregost inn" in the same scene. It didn't break anything, but it made me unsure where Pell was standing for a moment.
- Pell's Perception rolls took three tries to get through. That was fine, but it might be worth saying up front how much a clear read of the square costs in time, so the player can choose to push or wait.
- I'd like a clearer sense of what the hooded man's tools and stained sleeve point toward. I'm happy to leave it as a thread, but a tiny bit more would help me decide whether Pell should follow it or let it go.

Overall: I'd sit down at this table again.

private.text: You stay in the mouth of the lane, the stacked barrels making a dark place at your back. Past them the street is going blue with dusk. Lamps are being lit one by one along the forge row, and the smith's stall at the edge of the square is shuttering its last board. You need to know who out there is watching the Burning Wizard's door, and you have to read the street before the light is gone.

Out of game: the card is waiting for you. Press [Onward] to take the result as it fell, or use one of your session rerolls on Perception if you want to cast the die again. Pell crouching behind the barrels is taken as his position; what he sees of the square is decided when the card resolves.

The Perception card is still waiting. Press Onward to take the roll as it fell, or spend one of your session rerolls on it. Your description of the square is a proposal, and what Pell actually makes out of it will be settled when the card resolves.

You crouch and look under the barrels. There is a split sack, a wedge of dry straw, and a rat that decides you are not worth the trouble. You stay low a moment longer, and from there the square opens up past the stack.

Across the square a man leans on the horse trough by the smith's stall. He wears a dark cloak with the collar turned up, and his boots are good leather, not the Fist's issue. He isn't drinking and isn't talking to anyone. He watches the Burning Wizard's shutters for longer than anyone waits on a friend. When the stall-keeper drags a board across to close up, the man's head turns toward the noise and then back to the inn. He lifts one hand from his cloak and rubs his thumb over something on his finger, and a small glint catches the lamp at the corner. Then he pushes off the trough and walks east toward the forge row, not hurrying.

You watch him as far as the last lamp, then get up from the barrels. The stall-keeper is still at his board. You put a silver on the counter and give him a hard look. He takes the coin without a word, hands over a flask of oil, and bolts the shutter behind him.

The card is still waiting for you. Press Roll the die: Pell's Perception decides how much of the square and the man on the low wall he actually makes out, including the ring and the cloak. Following him at a distance will be settled from what the roll gives Pell to work with. The flask of oil comes from Pell's own satchel, so that stands.

The cloaked man's ring catches the lantern once more as he turns away from the cooper's yard, and then the dusk takes the light and both men with it. Pell has seen what there was to see: the nod, the hand turned palm-down, the glance back toward the square that passed over the water butt without stopping.

The hooded man in the drover's tabard does not look back at all. He goes north up the forge row toward the Fist's lodging, his stride even and unhurried. Where the sleeve has fallen back at the wrist, the cloth is dark. Ink, perhaps, if he keeps tallies for a carter. Or something a day old that has not yet washed out. The belt of tools at his hip is kept too neatly for a drover: every loop full, every buckle polished.

The cloaked man goes on east, past the cooper's, toward the end of the row where the lanes thin into fields and the road for the south-east fields leaves the town. He does not hurry. Twice he stops where a shuttered window throws a line of light across the cobbles, and each time he waits, as if for someone who has not yet come.

Pell is still at the water butt, the cold of the stone coming through his coat. Two ways open from here. The cloaked man is heading out past the last houses, where a man can be gone in a minute. The hooded man is walking toward the Fist, where a tradesman with neat tools and a stained cuff would be asked a great many questions if anyone stopped him.

Which of them does Pell follow?

Three travellers have come in by three roads and found the same table. Bram Halloway walked up the Coast Way from Nashkel with the dust of the road still on his boots. Sefa Marrin came up from Baldur's Gate by the Trade Way. Pell Dunmore arrived from the west by the High Hedge road. None of them knows the others yet, and each has reasons for being here that the others have not heard. Behind the bar, the proprietor Doran Quill sets down a cup and looks from one face to the next, as if waiting to see who will speak first. Outside, the forge hammers have fallen silent for the day, and the street beyond the shutters is going dim. What happens at this table is still undecided.
